source.question: e-10687
source.value:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{1+x^2} \, \textrm{d}x = \arctan(x) + C
$$

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a \to -\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =4\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)]_{a}^{0} \\  & =4\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(a)] \\  & =4\cdot (0-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(a)]) \\  & =-4{lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(a)]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y = \arctan{x},$ shown in the graph below:

- $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \left[\arctan{x}\right] = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

- $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \left[\arctan{x}\right] = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039465/assets/27ec65761e5119be666e69b67b2fa2fcb7b4f3665ddc41faddd6c136d5c955b1.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =-4{lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(a)] \\  & =-4(-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

source.value:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{1+(kx)^2} \, \textrm dx = \dfrac{1}{k} \arctan \left(kx \right) + C
$$

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1/4}^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+16{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{-1/4}^{a}\frac{1}{1+16{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{-1/4}^{a}\frac{1}{1+(4x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(4x)]}_{-1/4}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(4a)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(4a)]-(-\frac{\pi }{4})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(4a)]+\frac{\pi }{4})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\arctan{(4x)},$ shown in the graph below:

- $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \left[\arctan{(4x)}\right] = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

- $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \left[\arctan{(4x)}\right] = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039465/assets/9a7272f8bc8d0eba3e5bfc38e843cd02db3f3eb7b51e77b95b2efd61034890b6.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1/4}^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+16{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(4a)]+\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

source.value:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{k^2 + x^2} \, \textrm dx = \dfrac{1}{k} \arctan \left( \dfrac{x}{k} \right) + C
$$

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2\sqrt{3}}^{\infty }\frac{6}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x & =6\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2\sqrt{3}}^{a}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2\sqrt{3}}^{a}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{2}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{2})]}_{2\sqrt{3}}^{a} \\  & =3{lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{2})-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3})) \\  & =3{lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{2})-\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =3{lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{2})]-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right),$ shown in the graph below:

- $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \left[\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\right] = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

- $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \left[\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\right] = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039465/assets/042ad2450306552d9d5a7e4219d15547ad7104601b7ce6350a64193981de0de7.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2\sqrt{3}}^{\infty }\frac{6}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x & =3{lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{2})]-\pi  \\  & =3\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}-\pi  \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

source.question: e-10688
source.value:
First, we substitute $u = x^2.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 2x
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}u =2x \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Since $u \to \infty$ when $x \to \infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u = x^2$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $\infty$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\infty$ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{2x}{1+{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{2x}{1+{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(u)]_{1}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(a)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)] \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(a)]-\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\arctan(x),$ shown in the graph below:

- $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \left[ \arctan(x) \right] = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

- $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \left[ \arctan(x) \right] = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039465/assets/46e6cf2950c99831a7445a862fb36a6a7b8f9233a82e49c7cf5da4a383ec4756.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{2x}{1+{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(a)]-\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
